runtime cost of boxing every value as an object

candidates.quote: One of my goals for Python was to make it so that all objects were "first class." By this, I meant that I wanted all objects that could be named in the language ... to have equal status.
candidates.statement: Make every object that can be named a first-class citizen with equal status: assignable, passable, storable, callable.

strongest.why: collapsing the hierarchy of citizen-kinds into one equal status reorganizes how one thinks about what a value is, so functions, classes and types become ordinary things to pass and store

candidates.above_next: a stance on what the language must never do cuts deeper than a stance about sparing the user implementation trivia

also.why: it unifies all failure into one mechanism, so there is never an undefined or garbage result to reason about

beats.why: checking overflow and raising rather than clipping is this rule applied to one operation, narrower than the rule itself

harms: forces callers to handle exceptions everywhere, more verbose control flow
a raise can abort a long computation that a sentinel would have let continue
hides no-value cases as control flow rather than data
candidates.instead_of: returning sentinels, undefined values or silently wrapped results that let an error pass unnoticed
candidates.quote: I decided that there should be no undefined result values in Python – instead, exceptions should always be raised when no correct return value can be computed.
candidates.statement: Never return an undefined or silently wrong value; raise an exception whenever no correct result can be computed.

strongest.why: it takes a stance that silence about failure is itself a failure: the language refuses to hand back a value it cannot justify

candidates.above_next: it is a rule about the whole user-facing surface, wider than the rule about unifying kinds under one concept

also.why: the word 'violated' shows an author who feels the philosophy as an obligation he's ashamed to have broken

beats.why: refusing instance-variable declarations is one case of sparing the user, not the general rule, so it infects less

harms: hiding the implementation can cost performance the user can't then control
the line of what counts as 'uninteresting' is the designer's, not the user's
leaky abstractions bite harder when the detail was meant to be invisible
candidates.instead_of: requiring markers, suffixes or declarations that exist only to serve the implementation
candidates.quote: This is one area where Python violated the ABC-inspired philosophy of not requiring users to care about a uninteresting implementation details.
candidates.statement: Don't make users care about uninteresting implementation details.

strongest.why: it is a position on whose convenience the language serves: the programmer's attention, not the implementer's bookkeeping

candidates.above_next: finding the concept behind many types reorganizes the frame more than the method constraint of not inventing syntax

also.why: len, indexing, slicing and iteration reading the same on every sequence is an economy a reader feels at once

harms: forces unrelated types into one interface that may not fit all of them

duck typing lets a wrong object pass if it happens to answer the same operations
candidates.instead_of: giving each type its own separate operations with their own names and behavior
candidates.quote: I decided to generalize these to a common concept, the sequence. This generalization made it so certain core operations such as getting the length (len(s)), indexing (s[i]), slicing (s[i:j]), and iteration (for i in s) worked the same on any sequence type.
candidates.statement: When several types share operations, generalize them to one common concept so the same operations work the same on all.

strongest.why: naming the shared concept behind list, tuple and string reframes operations as belonging to a protocol, not to a type, the seed of Python's whole protocol style

candidates.above_next: a restraint running through the whole grammar outranks a single aesthetic rule about one data type's printed form

also.why: a stance that the language stays small on purpose, that new syntax is a debt the whole community pays

beats.why: holding descriptors back until syntax could follow is one instance of the restraint, not the standing rule to prefer the minimal no-new-syntax solution

harms: overloading one syntax for many roles can hide important distinctions from the reader
refusing new syntax forces awkward conventions (self, __dunder__, decorators by assignment) onto users
'minimal' for the implementer can mean surprising for the learner
candidates.instead_of: inventing dedicated syntax for each new feature (a method keyword, operator declarations, a metaclass clause)
candidates.quote: A major design constraint was that I didn't want to add syntax for methods that differed from the syntax for functions. Refactoring the grammar and the byte code generator to handle such similar cases differently felt like a huge task.
candidates.statement: Prefer the minimal solution that reuses existing constructs; don't add new syntax when an existing one will do.

strongest.why: it is a discipline of economy: reach the feature with the construct you already have rather than growing the grammar

candidates.above_next: a rule covering every data type's representation reaches further than one chosen indexing convention

also.why: it ties display to the parser, so the reader learns a type's syntax just by printing a value of it

harms: forces ugly compromises (the trailing comma for one-tuples) to keep output parseable
not every object has a sensible literal form, so the rule can't always hold
a faithful repr can leak internals the user shouldn't rely on
candidates.instead_of: printing values in an ad-hoc display form that can't be read back as code
candidates.quote: One of the rules I took from ABC was that every data type, when printed or converted to a string, should be represented by an expression that was a valid input to the language's parser.
candidates.statement: Make a value's printed representation an expression that is valid input to the parser.

strongest.why: a value's printed form being valid input back into the language is a clean closure, the output and the source made one

also.why: it reframes indexing around the invariant between slices rather than the position of elements, so corrections (+1/-1) disappear

beats.why: flooring integer division to satisfy a math relation is a kindred beauty-of-the-invariant choice but touches one operator, narrower

harms: 0-based half-open trips up people from 1-based math and everyday counting
the elegance argument can override what a given domain finds natural
off-by-one still bites when the invariant isn't internalized
candidates.instead_of: 1-based indexing with closed intervals that force awkward +1/-1 compensation on everyday slicing
candidates.quote: the invariant that when two / slices are adjacent, the first slice's end index is the second slice's / start index is just too beautiful to ignore.
candidates.statement: Choose the convention whose invariant makes the common cases come out clean, without +1/-1 corrections.

strongest.why: choosing the convention because adjacent slices share an index is 'too beautiful to ignore', design settled by the beauty of the invariant
